error_modes.label: ALTITUDE control during and after recovery

texts.0: SP, due to a delayed pitch input after the nose-low entry followed by an abrupt over-rotation, failed to arrest the descent near the entry altitude and then ballooned while chasing it back. Level flight was established more than 300 ft from the target altitude, outside the maximum tolerance. The IP intervened on the controls to stop the excursion. The requirement to recover with the minimum loss of altitude was not met.
texts.1: SP, due to a shallow initial recovery pitch attitude that was held too long, allowed the altitude excursion to build to about 300 ft, at the limit of the tolerance. SP started the correction only after verbal prompting from the IP and returned to the target altitude late. No control intervention was required, but the recovery did not meet the minimum-loss-of-altitude requirement.
texts.2: SP, due to an initially insufficient pull during the nose-low recovery, let the altitude excursion reach roughly 200 ft, between the desired and the maximum tolerance. SP recognized the trend on the altimeter and the VVI and corrected it without prompting, establishing level flight promptly. The excursion stayed inside the 300 ft limit throughout.
texts.3: SP arrested the excursion early and established level flight within 150 ft of the target altitude on every recovery. The pitch correction was smooth and applied as soon as the attitude was identified, so the altitude stayed inside the desired band.
texts.4: SP recovered with almost no measurable altitude excursion, holding level flight within a few tens of feet of the target altitude. The initial pitch input was sized correctly on the first attempt, so no secondary correction was needed on any repetition.
texts.marginal: SP kept the altitude excursion inside standards on each recovery, but the values clustered near the outer part of the desired band and were consistently in the same direction, undershooting the level-off. The trend comes from recognizing the level-off point slightly late rather than from control technique. SP is expected to anticipate the level-off earlier so that the excursions settle nearer the target altitude.

texts_at.0: With the IP flying the entry into the unusual attitude and calling the pitch input for the recovery, SP followed the pitch input called on the early repetitions. The recovery pitch attitude for this type of entry has not yet been learned, so the correction is still applied on a call rather than sized to the attitude seen. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin sizing the initial pitch input independently as more entries are flown.
texts_at.1: SP started the correction only after verbal prompting from the IP, with the excursion building to about 300 ft, at the limit of the tolerance, because the initial recovery pitch attitude had been shallow and held too long. The return to the target altitude was late once the prompting had been given. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to size the initial pitch input correctly without needing the correction prompted.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the trend on the altimeter and the VVI and corrected it without prompting, establishing level flight promptly, after an initially insufficient pull during the nose-low recovery let the altitude excursion reach roughly 200 ft, between the desired and the maximum tolerance. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to size the initial pull correctly rather than correcting it after the trend is seen.
texts_at.3: SP arrested the excursion early and established level flight within 150 ft of the target altitude on every recovery, applying the pitch correction smoothly and as soon as the attitude was identified so the altitude stayed inside the desired band. One recovery arrested the excursion a beat later than the others. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring every recovery to the same promptness as the earliest one.

texts_above.1: SP corrected the recovery pitch attitude, containing the altitude excursion to about 300 ft, at the limit of the tolerance. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the trend on the altimeter and the VVI and corrected it without prompting, establishing level flight promptly and holding the excursion to roughly 200 ft, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, after an initially insufficient pull during the nose-low recovery. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good altitude control during and after recovery.
texts_above.3: SP arrested the excursion early and established level flight within 150 ft of the target altitude on every recovery of the sortie, applying the pitch correction smoothly and as soon as the attitude was identified. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise altitude control during and after recovery.
texts_above.4: SP recovered with almost no measurable altitude excursion, holding level flight within a few tens of feet of the target altitude on every repetition, sizing the initial pitch input correctly on the first attempt so no secondary correction was ever needed. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless altitude control during and after recovery.

texts.0: SP, due to inadequate monitoring of airspeed while attention stayed on the attitude indicator, left the power lever untouched during the nose-low recovery. Airspeed diverged more than 20 KIAS from the target, outside the maximum tolerance and toward the aircraft limitation, and the IP retarded the power to contain it. The control and performance technique required for the recovery was not applied.
texts.1: SP, due to an interrupted cross-check that omitted the airspeed indicator once the attitude was corrected, delayed the power adjustment until the IP called the trend. The excursion reached about 20 KIAS, at the tolerance limit, before it was contained. The recovery was completed without control intervention, but only after verbal prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a power adjustment made after the pitch input rather than together with it, allowed airspeed to diverge about 15 KIAS from the target, between the desired and the maximum tolerance. SP picked the trend up in the cross-check and corrected it without prompting. Airspeed was back inside the desired band before level flight was stabilized.
texts.3: SP set power together with the pitch and bank correction, so airspeed stayed within 10 KIAS of the target on both nose-high and nose-low recoveries. The airspeed indicator was part of the cross-check from the first moment of the recovery.
texts.4: SP anticipated the airspeed change from the entry attitude and positioned power accordingly, keeping the excursion to a few knots. Airspeed was stable at the target value as level flight was established, with no secondary power correction.
texts.marginal: SP held airspeed inside standards, but the excursions repeatedly reached the outer part of the desired band on the nose-low entries, where the trend builds fastest. The power input is being made just after the pitch input instead of with it. SP is expected to make the power change part of the initial recovery action so that airspeed stays closer to the target.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling the airspeed trend during the recovery, SP adjusted power on the call given. The airspeed indicator has not yet been built into the recovery cross-check, so a power adjustment is still made on a call rather than on SP's own scan. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin keeping the airspeed indicator in the cross-check without the trend being called.
texts_at.1: SP had the excursion contained only after the IP called the trend, with airspeed reaching about 20 KIAS and altitude up to 300 ft from the assigned level, at the tolerance limit, because the cross-check had omitted the airspeed indicator once the attitude had been corrected. The recovery was completed once the trend had been called, though only after verbal prompting. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to keep the airspeed indicator in the cross-check without needing the trend called.
texts_at.2: SP picked the trend up in the cross-check and corrected it without prompting, bringing airspeed back inside the desired band before level flight was stabilized, after a power adjustment made after the pitch input rather than with it let airspeed diverge about 15 KIAS and altitude about 250 ft from the assigned level. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to make the power adjustment with the pitch input rather than after it.
texts_at.3: SP set power together with the pitch and bank correction on both nose-high and nose-low recoveries, so airspeed stayed within 10 KIAS of the target and altitude within 150 ft of the assigned level, with the airspeed indicator part of the cross-check from the first moment of the recovery. One recovery let the airspeed edge toward the outer part of the band before it was checked. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring every recovery to the same tightness as the cleanest one.

texts_above.1: SP brought the airspeed indicator back into the cross-check during the recovery, containing the excursion to about 20 KIAS, at the tolerance limit. That correction came after a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP picked up the trend in the cross-check and corrected it without prompting, bringing airspeed back inside the desired band before level flight was stabilized, holding the deviation to about 15 KIAS, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, after a power adjustment made a moment after the pitch input. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound airspeed control during recovery.
texts_above.3: SP set power together with the pitch and bank correction on every recovery of the sortie, so airspeed stayed within 10 KIAS of the target on both nose-high and nose-low entries with the airspeed indicator part of the cross-check from the first moment. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed airspeed control during recovery.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated the airspeed change from the entry attitude and positioned power accordingly on every recovery, keeping the excursion to a few knots with airspeed stable at the target value as level flight was established and no secondary power correction ever needed. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior airspeed control during recovery.

error_modes.label: HEADING on completion of the recovery

texts.0: SP, due to taking the roll-out reference from the turn needle instead of the attitude indicator and the HSI, stopped the recovery on a heading more than 10 deg from the target. SP then hunted the heading with alternating bank inputs and the IP took the controls to stabilize the aircraft. The requirement to recover to level flight on the intended heading was not met.
texts.1: SP, due to rolling the wings level without checking the HSI, finished the recovery about 10 deg off the target heading, at the tolerance limit. The error was corrected only after the IP pointed it out, and the correction itself was flown with excess bank. No control intervention was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly late roll-out from the recovery bank, ended up about 8 deg from the target heading, between the desired and the maximum tolerance. SP identified the error on the HSI without prompting and closed it with a coordinated turn at a suitable bank angle. Heading was inside the desired band before the maneuver was terminated.
texts.3: SP rolled out within 5 deg of the target heading on each recovery, using the attitude indicator for the roll-out and the HSI to confirm it. No heading hunting followed the recovery.
texts.4: SP completed each recovery essentially on heading, with deviations of a degree or two. The roll-out was anticipated so that the wings came level exactly as the target heading arrived, on entries with small and large bank angles alike.
texts.marginal: SP kept heading inside standards, but the roll-outs finished consistently near the edge of the desired band and always in the direction of the recovery turn. The roll-out is being started at the target heading rather than before it. SP is expected to lead the roll-out so that the aircraft settles closer to the intended heading.

texts_at.0: With the IP pointing out the heading error at roll-out, SP corrected the heading pointed out. The habit of checking the HSI at roll-out from an unusual attitude has not yet been built, so the wings are still rolled level without a heading check until the error is pointed out. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to begin checking the HSI at roll-out without the error being pointed out.
texts_at.1: SP had the error corrected only after the IP pointed it out, finishing about 10 deg off the target heading, at the tolerance limit, because the roll-out had been made without checking the HSI. The correction itself was flown with excess bank once it was pointed out. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to check the HSI at roll-out without needing the error pointed out.
texts_at.2: SP identified the error on the HSI without prompting and closed it with a coordinated turn at a suitable bank angle, after a slightly late roll-out from the recovery bank left the aircraft about 8 deg from the target heading, between the desired and the maximum tolerance. Heading was inside the desired band before the maneuver was terminated. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to start the roll-out a beat earlier so the error does not develop.
texts_at.3: SP rolled out within 5 deg of the target heading on every recovery, using the attitude indicator for the roll-out and the HSI to confirm it, with no heading hunting following the recovery. One roll-out was judged a touch wider than the others before it settled. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to judge every roll-out as precisely as the tightest one.

texts_above.1: SP finished the recovery on the HSI, containing the heading error to about 10 deg off the target heading, at the tolerance limit. The IP's verbal call preceded the correction. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP identified an error on the HSI without prompting and closed it with a coordinated turn at a suitable bank angle, holding the deviation to about 8 deg, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, after a slightly late roll-out from the recovery bank. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady heading control on completion of the recovery.
texts_above.3: SP rolled out within 5 deg of the target heading on every recovery of the sortie, using the attitude indicator for the roll-out and the HSI to confirm it, with no heading hunting following any recovery. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed heading control on completion of the recovery.
texts_above.4: SP completed each recovery essentially on heading, with deviations of a degree or two on entries with small and large bank angles alike, anticipating the roll-out so the wings came level exactly as the target heading arrived. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary heading control on completion of the recovery.

error_modes.label: Recognition and identification of the unusual attitude

texts.0: SP, due to a startle response at the entry that displaced the memorized recovery sequence, did not identify whether the attitude was nose-high or nose-low before moving the controls. SP applied a nose-low recovery input to a nose-high attitude, aggravating the situation, and the IP took the controls. The requirement to recognize the type of unusual attitude timely and correctly was not met.
texts.1: SP, due to surprise at the entry, hesitated on the attitude indicator and identified the attitude only after the IP prompted a call. The recovery that followed was correct in type but started several seconds late, so the resulting excursions reached the outer tolerances. No control intervention was needed.
texts.2: SP, due to a short startle-related pause before transitioning to the attitude indicator, identified the attitude marginally late but correctly and without prompting. The recovery inputs were then applied in the right order. The delay produced excursions between the desired and the maximum tolerances and nothing beyond that.
texts.3: SP recognized the type of unusual attitude immediately at the entry and called it correctly, then applied the matching recovery sequence. The identification was based on the attitude indicator cross-checked with the airspeed and altimeter trends.
texts.4: SP identified nose-high and nose-low entries instantly and correctly on every repetition, including entries with large bank angles. The identification and the first recovery input were effectively simultaneous, with no hesitation between them.
texts.marginal: SP identified every entry correctly and within standards, but the identification took noticeably longer on the entries with high bank angle than on the near wings-level ones. The pause suggests the attitude is still being reasoned out rather than recognized at once. SP is expected to bring the recognition time down so that it is uniform regardless of the entry attitude.

texts_at.0: With the IP prompting SP to call the attitude on the entry, SP identified the attitude on the prompt given. The recognition of an unusual attitude on first exposure is still slowed by the surprise of the entry itself, so identification is still prompted rather than called independently. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin calling the attitude on recognition without it being prompted.
texts_at.1: SP identified the attitude only after the IP prompted a call, because surprise at the entry had caused hesitation on the attitude indicator. The recovery that followed was correct in type but started several seconds late, so the resulting excursions reached 300 ft and 10 degrees at the outer tolerances. No control intervention was needed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to call the attitude on recognition without needing it prompted.
texts_at.2: SP identified the attitude marginally late but correctly and without prompting, after a short startle-related pause before transitioning to the attitude indicator, then applied the recovery inputs in the right order. The delay produced excursions of about 200 ft and 8 degrees, between the desired and the maximum tolerances, and nothing beyond that. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to shorten the pause before the transition to the attitude indicator.
texts_at.3: SP recognized the type of unusual attitude immediately at the entry and called it correctly, then applied the matching recovery sequence, basing the identification on the attitude indicator cross-checked with the airspeed and altimeter trends and holding the resulting excursions inside 150 ft and 5 degrees. One entry took a beat longer to identify than the others. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring every identification to the same speed as the quickest one.

texts_above.1: SP identified the unusual attitude and flew the correct type of recovery, though the identification itself took several seconds and the resulting excursions reached the outer tolerances. A verbal call from the IP came before the correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP identified the attitude marginally late but correctly and without prompting, after a short startle-related pause before transitioning to the attitude indicator, then applied the recovery inputs in the right order with excursions staying between the desired and the maximum tolerances. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable recognition and identification of the unusual attitude.
texts_above.3: SP recognized the type of unusual attitude immediately at every entry and called it correctly, then applied the matching recovery sequence, basing the identification on the attitude indicator cross-checked with the airspeed and altimeter trends. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good recognition and identification of the unusual attitude.
texts_above.4: SP identified nose-high and nose-low entries instantly and correctly on every repetition, including entries with large bank angles, with identification and the first recovery input effectively simultaneous and no hesitation between them. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior recognition and identification of the unusual attitude.

texts.0: SP, due to applying the recovery actions out of sequence, pulled toward the horizon on the nose-high entry before unloading and rolling, and let the airspeed decay to the onset of buffet. The aircraft was flown to the edge of a stall and the IP took the controls to recover it. The requirement to recover without flying the aircraft into a stall was not met.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete recovery sequence on the nose-low entry, rolled and pulled without first reducing power, so the pull had to be prolonged and the excursions reached the outer tolerances. SP completed the missing action only after the IP called it. The aircraft stayed within its limitations and no control intervention was required.
texts.2: SP, due to performing the roll and the pitch input in partial overlap instead of in the correct order, made the recovery less efficient and needed a second correction to settle the aircraft. SP recognized the error and completed the sequence correctly without prompting. All resulting excursions stayed between the desired and the maximum tolerances.
texts.3: SP applied the correct recovery sequence for each entry type, setting power and unloading or rolling as required, and returned the aircraft to level flight in a continuous, controlled action. No step was omitted or reordered.
texts.4: SP flew each recovery as a single smooth sequence with correctly sized inputs and needed no secondary correction on any repetition. The technique was identical for nose-high and nose-low entries and unaffected by the bank angle at the entry.
texts.marginal: SP used the correct sequence throughout, but the individual actions were made one at a time with a visible gap between them, which lengthened the recovery. The technique is sound and the standards were met on every repetition. SP is expected to blend the actions into one continuous recovery so that the aircraft returns to level flight faster.

texts_at.0: With the IP naming the missing step of the recovery sequence, SP completed the action named. The recovery sequence for a nose-low entry has not yet been learned as a single flow, so a step, such as the power reduction, is still supplied by the IP rather than included from memory. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to begin including every step of the sequence without one being named.
texts_at.1: SP completed the missing action only after the IP called it, because an incomplete recovery sequence on the nose-low entry had rolled and pulled without first reducing power, prolonging the pull and letting the excursions reach 300 ft, at the outer tolerance. The aircraft stayed within its limitations and no control intervention was required. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to include every step of the sequence without needing one called.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the error and completed the sequence correctly without prompting, after performing the roll and the pitch input in partial overlap instead of in the correct order made the recovery less efficient and needed a second correction to settle the aircraft. The resulting excursions reached about 250 ft and stayed between the desired and the maximum tolerances. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to keep roll and pitch fully sequenced rather than overlapping them.
texts_at.3: SP applied the correct recovery sequence for each entry type, setting power and unloading or rolling as required, returning the aircraft to level flight within 150 ft of the entry altitude in a continuous, controlled action with no step omitted or reordered. One recovery needed the sequence steps spaced a moment further apart than the others. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring every recovery to the same continuity as the smoothest one.

texts_above.1: SP completed the recovery sequence on the nose-low entry, including the power reduction, and kept the excursions within the outer tolerances of the recovery. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized an error and completed the sequence correctly without prompting, after performing the roll and the pitch input in partial overlap made the recovery less efficient, needing only a second correction and no IP input to settle the aircraft. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid recovery technique and sequencing.
texts_above.3: SP applied the correct recovery sequence for each entry type on every repetition, setting power and unloading or rolling as required and returning the aircraft to level flight in a continuous, controlled action with no step omitted or reordered. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate recovery technique and sequencing.
texts_above.4: SP flew each recovery as a single smooth sequence with correctly sized inputs and needed no secondary correction on any repetition, with the technique identical for nose-high and nose-low entries and unaffected by the bank angle at the entry. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary recovery technique and sequencing.

error_modes.label: Aircraft limitations and promptness without IP intervention

texts.0: SP, due to an over-aggressive pull during the nose-low recovery, exceeded the load limitation for the configuration while the airspeed was still increasing. The IP took the controls to unload the aircraft and complete the recovery. The requirement to recover without exceeding the aircraft limitations was not met.
texts.1: SP, due to a pull applied at a rate that brought the aircraft to the onset of buffet, left almost no margin to the limitation, and the IP had to call for the pull to be eased. SP responded to the verbal correction and the recovery was completed without control intervention. The recovery was neither prompt nor flown with an adequate margin.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly excessive initial pull, produced a load and an airspeed trend that had to be adjusted during the recovery. SP eased the input without prompting after seeing the trend and completed the recovery with an adequate margin to the limits. No intervention was required and the excursions stayed inside the maximum tolerances.
texts.3: SP recovered promptly on every entry with the pull kept inside the load and airspeed limits, so the aircraft was never taken near a stall or an overspeed. The recoveries were completed without any prompting or intervention from the IP.
texts.4: SP recovered each entry at the fastest rate the limitations allow, using the available margin fully but never approaching it. The aircraft was returned to level flight quickly with the load and the airspeed under continuous control.
texts.marginal: SP stayed inside the aircraft limits on every recovery, but the nose-low pulls were consistently flown with a load close to the upper part of the usable range. The result met the standards, yet the margin left for an entry with a steeper attitude is small. SP is expected to size the pull with more margin while keeping the recovery prompt.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling for the pull to be eased as the aircraft approached the onset of buffet, SP eased the pull on the call given. The margin to the aircraft limitation at the initial pull has not yet been judged independently, so the rate is still eased on a call rather than set with a margin from the outset. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin leaving a wider margin at the initial pull without it being eased by a call.
texts_at.1: SP responded to the verbal correction from the IP, with a pull applied at a rate that brought the aircraft to the onset of buffet, leaving almost no margin to the limitation, and airspeed reached 20 KIAS from the entry value, at the limit of the standard, before the pull was eased. The recovery was completed without control intervention, but only on the call from the front cockpit, and was neither prompt nor flown with an adequate margin. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to leave a wider margin at the initial pull without needing it eased.
texts_at.2: SP eased the input without prompting after seeing the trend and completed the recovery with an adequate margin to the limits, after a slightly excessive initial pull produced a load and an airspeed trend that had to be adjusted during the recovery. No intervention was required and the excursions stayed at about 200 ft, inside the maximum tolerance. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to size the initial pull with the margin already built in.
texts_at.3: SP recovered promptly on every entry with the pull kept inside the load and airspeed limits, so the aircraft was never taken near a stall or an overspeed and altitude was regained within 150 ft of the entry level, with the recoveries completed without any prompting or intervention from the IP. One recovery used a pull a shade closer to the limit than the others. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring every pull to the same margin as the most conservative one.

texts_above.1: SP completed the recovery without control intervention, though the initial pull left almost no margin to the load limitation. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP to ease the pull. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP eased the input without prompting after seeing the trend, completing the recovery with an adequate margin to the limits after a slightly excessive initial pull had produced a load and an airspeed trend needing adjustment. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good control within aircraft limitations and prompt recovery.
texts_above.3: SP recovered promptly on every entry with the pull kept inside the load and airspeed limits on the whole sortie, so the aircraft was never taken near a stall or an overspeed and no recovery needed prompting or intervention from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined control within aircraft limitations and prompt recovery.
texts_above.4: SP recovered each entry at the fastest rate the limitations allow, using the available margin fully but never approaching it, with the aircraft returned to level flight quickly and the load and the airspeed under continuous control throughout. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding control within aircraft limitations and prompt recovery.

texts.0: SP, due to a false attitude perception that was not resolved against the instruments, flew the recovery on physical sensation instead of the attitude indicator and rolled in the wrong direction. The aircraft was taken further into the unusual attitude and the IP took the controls. The requirement to use the correct instrument flight references was not met.
texts.1: SP, due to conflicting attitude sensations that were left unresolved, fixated on the attitude indicator and did not bring the performance instruments into the cross-check. The resulting altitude and airspeed excursions reached the tolerance limits and were corrected only after the IP prompted them. No control intervention was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a short period of false attitude perception at the entry, delayed the transition to a full cross-check and initially referred only to the control instruments. SP resolved the sensation against the instruments without prompting and reintegrated the performance instruments, keeping the excursions between the desired and the maximum tolerances.
texts.3: SP used the control instruments to establish the recovery attitude and power and the performance instruments to confirm the result, in accordance with the applicable instrument flight procedures. The cross-check remained continuous through the recovery and no attitude sensation was acted on without instrument confirmation.
texts.4: SP maintained a complete and evenly distributed cross-check throughout every recovery, with no fixation on any single instrument. Control and performance instruments were used exactly as intended and the recoveries were flown entirely on instrument reference regardless of the entry attitude.
texts.marginal: SP used the correct instrument references and met the standards, but the cross-check narrowed to the attitude indicator for the first seconds of each recovery before widening again. Nothing was missed, although the performance instruments were brought back in later than ideal. SP is expected to keep the full cross-check running from the moment the entry is recognized.

texts_at.0: With the IP prompting the performance instruments into the cross-check, SP brought them into the scan on the prompt given. The transition from the attitude indicator to the performance instruments has not yet been learned, so attention is still fixated on the attitude indicator until the IP prompts the wider scan. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin bringing the performance instruments into the cross-check without them being prompted.
texts_at.1: SP had the excursions corrected only after the IP prompted them, because attention had fixated on the attitude indicator and the performance instruments had not been brought into the cross-check, letting altitude reach 300 ft and airspeed 20 KIAS at the tolerance limits. No control intervention was required. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to bring the performance instruments into the cross-check without needing them prompted.
texts_at.2: SP resolved the sensation against the instruments without prompting and reintegrated the performance instruments, keeping the excursions to about 250 ft, between the desired and the maximum tolerances, after a short period of false attitude perception at the entry delayed the transition to a full cross-check. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to shorten the delay before reintegrating the performance instruments.
texts_at.3: SP used the control instruments to establish the recovery attitude and power and the performance instruments to confirm the result, in accordance with the applicable instrument flight procedures, so altitude was held within 150 ft of the entry level with the cross-check continuous through the recovery and no attitude sensation acted on without instrument confirmation. One recovery brought the performance instruments in a beat later than the others. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring every recovery to the same cross-check speed as the quickest one.

texts_above.1: SP brought the performance instruments into the cross-check during the recovery, containing the altitude and airspeed excursions to the tolerance limits. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP resolved a false sensation against the instruments without prompting and reintegrated the performance instruments, keeping the excursions between the desired and the maximum tolerances, after a short period of false attitude perception at the entry delayed the full cross-check. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent instrument cross-check and use of control and performance references.
texts_above.3: SP used the control instruments to establish the recovery attitude and power and the performance instruments to confirm the result on every recovery, in accordance with the applicable instrument flight procedures, with the cross-check continuous throughout and no attitude sensation acted on without instrument confirmation. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed instrument cross-check and use of control and performance references.
texts_above.4: SP maintained a complete and evenly distributed cross-check throughout every recovery, with no fixation on any single instrument, using control and performance instruments exactly as intended and flying entirely on instrument reference regardless of the entry attitude. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior instrument cross-check and use of control and performance references.

error_modes.label: Confirm step - EADI validity checked against standby ADI and performance instruments

texts.0: SP, due to recovering on the EADI without first verifying its proper operation, skipped the confirm step and never compared the EADI with the standby attitude indicator and the performance instruments. SP flew a recovery based on an indication that did not agree with the airspeed and altimeter trends and drove the aircraft further from level flight, with altitude off by more than 300 ft and heading off by more than 10 degrees. The IP took the controls to recover the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to accepting the EADI indication without cross-confirming it against the standby attitude indicator, entered the recovery on an unconfirmed attitude and had to reverse part of the input once the performance instruments were finally read. The IP called for the confirmation step out loud before SP performed it. Level flight was regained about 300 ft from the entry altitude and about 10 degrees off heading, at the tolerance limits, with no control intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to a late confirm step, started the recovery on the EADI alone and brought the standby attitude indicator and the performance instruments into the comparison only after the first input. SP detected the mismatch and adjusted the recovery without prompting. The delay cost about 200 ft of altitude and left roughly 7 degrees of heading error before the aircraft was settled.
texts.3: SP recognized the unusual attitude, confirmed it by comparing the EADI with the standby attitude indicator and the performance instruments, and only then applied the recovery. The confirmation was completed without measurable delay and the recovery finished within 150 ft of altitude and 5 degrees of heading.
texts.4: SP ran recognize, confirm and recover as one continuous sequence on every entry, with the EADI checked against the standby attitude indicator and the performance instruments before any control input. Attitude, altitude and heading were resolved with negligible deviation and no step of the sequence was abbreviated.
texts.marginal: SP confirmed the EADI against the standby attitude indicator on every entry and stayed inside the standards, but the confirmation was made after the recovery input had already begun rather than before it. Deviations remained close to the desired values and nothing was misidentified. SP is expected to complete the confirm step before the first control input so the recovery is never based on an unverified indication.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling for the confirmation step to be performed out loud, SP cross-confirmed the EADI on the call given. The confirmation of the EADI against the standby attitude indicator has not yet been built into the entry, so the step is still called out by the IP rather than performed automatically. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to begin confirming the EADI against the standby indicator without it being called.
texts_at.1: SP performed the confirmation only after the IP called for it out loud, with level flight regained about 300 ft from the entry altitude and about 10 degrees off heading, at the tolerance limits, because the EADI indication had been accepted without cross-confirming it against the standby attitude indicator. No control intervention was needed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to confirm the EADI against the standby indicator without needing it called.
texts_at.2: SP detected a mismatch and adjusted the recovery without prompting, after a late confirm step started the recovery on the EADI alone and brought the standby attitude indicator and the performance instruments into the comparison only after the first input, costing about 200 ft of altitude and roughly 7 degrees of heading error before the aircraft was settled. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to bring the standby indicator into the comparison before the first input rather than after it.
texts_at.3: SP recognized the unusual attitude, confirmed it by comparing the EADI with the standby attitude indicator and the performance instruments, and only then applied the recovery, with the confirmation completed without measurable delay and the recovery finishing within 150 ft of altitude and 5 degrees of heading. One confirmation took a beat longer than the others. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring every confirmation to the same speed as the quickest one.

error_modes.label: Roll toward wings level before pull-up - pitch correction started beyond 90 degrees of bank

texts.0: SP, due to correcting pitch before rolling upright from an inverted diving attitude, started the pull while the bank was still beyond 90 degrees and pointed the nose further below the horizon. The altitude loss passed 300 ft with the airspeed increasing more than 20 kt above the entry value before the aircraft was rolled. The IP took the controls to unload the aircraft and complete the recovery.
texts.1: SP, due to beginning the pull-up before the bank was reduced below 90 degrees, converted part of the recovery into additional descent and had to hold the pull far longer than required. The IP called for wings level first, after which SP completed the recovery correctly. The altitude loss reached about 300 ft and the airspeed about 20 kt above the entry value, at the tolerance limits, without control intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to overlapping the pull with the roll while the bank was still near 90 degrees, made the first part of the recovery ineffective and needed a second, larger pitch input once the wings were closer to level. SP recognized the priority error and finished the recovery in the correct order without prompting. Altitude loss stayed around 200 ft with airspeed about 15 kt above the entry value.
texts.3: SP treated the roll toward wings level as the priority on the nose-low entries and started the pull-up only once the bank was less than 90 degrees. The recovery was completed in one continuous action with altitude loss inside 150 ft and airspeed inside 10 kt of the entry value.
texts.4: SP rolled toward wings level and timed the start of the pull-up precisely as the bank passed below 90 degrees on every nose-low entry, including the steepest ones. The pull was applied with the lift vector already usable, so the recovery cost only negligible altitude and airspeed.
texts.marginal: SP always rolled before pulling and met the standards, but on the steeper entries the pull was started just as the bank reached 90 degrees rather than clearly below it. Altitude loss stayed within tolerance while trending toward the larger values. SP is expected to establish a clearer margin below 90 degrees of bank before applying the pitch input.

SP is expected to begin reducing bank below 90 degrees before pulling without it being called.

error_modes.label: Amount of bank used in the recovery - more bank than required

texts.0: SP, due to using more bank than the recovery required, rolled the aircraft close to 90 degrees on an entry that needed only a shallow correction and then had to reverse the roll to stop the resulting turn. The heading ended more than 10 degrees from the recovery heading and the altitude more than 300 ft from the entry value. The IP intervened on the controls to stop the developing excursion.
texts.1: SP, due to applying a standard large bank angle on every entry instead of only as much as required, produced an unnecessary turn during the recovery and corrected it only after the IP pointed out the heading trend. The heading error reached about 10 degrees and the altitude excursion about 300 ft, at the maximum tolerances. No control intervention was needed.
texts.2: SP, due to rolling with more bank than the attitude called for, added heading change that had to be taken back during the same recovery. SP saw the heading trend on the performance instruments and reduced the bank without prompting. The heading error peaked around 7 degrees and the altitude excursion around 200 ft.
texts.3: SP used only as much bank as each entry required and did not apply large bank angles where a shallow roll was sufficient. The recoveries were completed with heading kept inside 5 degrees and altitude inside 150 ft of the target values.
texts.4: SP matched the bank to the entry attitude on every repetition, using the minimum roll needed to place the lift vector correctly. Heading and altitude at the completion of each recovery differed only negligibly from the target values.
texts.marginal: SP kept the roll inputs inside the standards, but consistently used somewhat more bank than the entry attitude required, so each recovery produced a small unwanted heading change. The corrections were made in time and the tolerances were met. SP is expected to size the bank to the actual attitude rather than defaulting to a large roll on every entry.

error_modes.label: Nose-low recovery - power reduction and speed brake as required

texts.0: SP, due to omitting the power reduction and the speed brake in the diving recovery, left the aircraft accelerating through the pull and did not control the airspeed at any point of the recovery. The airspeed passed more than 20 kt above the target value while the altitude loss passed 300 ft. The IP took the controls, reduced power and completed the recovery.
texts.1: SP, due to reducing power late and not extending the speed brake when it was required, allowed the acceleration in the dive to continue and had to extend the recovery to bleed the excess speed. SP acted on the drag devices only after the IP called for them. The airspeed reached about 20 kt above the target and the altitude excursion about 300 ft, at the tolerance limits, with no control intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed power reduction in the nose-low recovery, entered the pull with more speed than necessary and had to use the speed brake to stop the trend. SP recognized the acceleration on the airspeed indicator and acted without prompting. The airspeed peaked about 15 kt above the target and the altitude excursion stayed around 200 ft.
texts.3: SP reduced power at the start of each nose-low recovery and extended the speed brake where it was required, keeping the acceleration in the dive under control. The airspeed at the completion of the recovery was within 10 kt of the target and the altitude loss within 150 ft.
texts.4: SP set power and used the speed brake as part of the same action as the roll and the pull on every nose-low entry, so the airspeed never departed noticeably from the target. The drag devices were retracted and power restored as level flight was reached, without any secondary correction.
texts.marginal: SP reduced power and used the speed brake correctly on every nose-low entry and stayed within the standards, but the power lever was moved only after the roll was complete rather than together with it. The airspeed excursions were contained yet consistently on the high side. SP is expected to make the power reduction part of the first recovery action so the acceleration is limited from the start.

texts_at.0: With the IP calling for the power reduction and the speed brake to be extended, SP acted on the drag devices called for. The power reduction and the speed brake have not yet been learned as part of the first recovery action, so the drag devices are still treated as a separate step supplied by a call. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin bringing the power reduction into the first recovery action without it being called.

texts_at.2: SP recovered every nose-low entry without prompting, reducing power during the pull and using the speed brake to hold the peak airspeed to roughly 15 kt above the target and the altitude excursion near 200 ft. texts.0: SP, due to not using power as required to maintain the desired airspeed in the climbing recovery, let the airspeed decay until the nose continued below the horizon on its own. What began as a nose-high entry ended as an uncontrolled nose-low attitude with the altitude more than 300 ft from the entry value and the airspeed more than 20 kt from the target. The IP took the controls to recover the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to adding power late in the nose-high recovery, allowed the airspeed to decay to the point where the nose fell through the horizon before the roll was complete, and the recovery had to be reflown from a nose-low attitude. SP advanced the power only after the IP called for it. The airspeed reached about 20 kt below the target and the altitude excursion about 300 ft, without control intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to a hesitant power application in the climbing recovery, let the airspeed decay further than necessary before the trend was arrested. SP advanced the power without prompting once the airspeed trend was seen and the nose was kept under control through the horizon. The airspeed low point was about 15 kt below the target and the altitude excursion about 200 ft.
texts.3: SP used power as required through each nose-high recovery so the airspeed stayed inside 10 kt of the target value and the nose was flown to the horizon rather than allowed to fall through it. The altitude excursion at the completion of the recovery stayed inside 150 ft.
texts.4: SP anticipated the airspeed decay on every nose-high entry and set power at the first recovery input, so the airspeed never approached a value at which the nose could fall through the horizon. Airspeed and altitude at the completion of each recovery differed only negligibly from the target values.
texts.marginal: SP applied power on every nose-high entry and kept the parameters inside the standards, but the input was made after the pitch and roll actions rather than with them, so each recovery included a period of decaying airspeed. Nothing exceeded the tolerances and the nose was always controlled. SP is expected to set power together with the first recovery input so the airspeed margin is preserved throughout.

error_modes.label: Use of the EADI presentation - fuselage dot to the horizon bar and the recovery chevrons

texts.0: SP, due to not reading the EADI presentation, ignored the recovery chevrons pointing to the horizon in the extreme attitude and never used the fuselage dot of the miniature aircraft in relation to the horizon bar. SP rolled in the wrong direction relative to the shortest way to the horizon and the aircraft ended more than 10 degrees off heading and more than 300 ft from the entry altitude. The IP took the controls.
texts.1: SP, due to disregarding the chevrons in the extreme nose-low entry, determined the direction of the horizon by trial rather than from the EADI presentation and rolled the long way round. The IP called the correct roll direction before SP corrected it. The heading ended about 10 degrees off and the altitude about 300 ft from the entry value, at the tolerance limits, with no control intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to reading the chevrons late, began the roll in an unclear direction and adjusted it once the fuselage dot and the horizon bar were interpreted correctly. The correction was made without prompting. The extra roll cost about 7 degrees of heading and about 200 ft of altitude.
texts.3: SP used the recovery chevrons to determine the attitude in the extreme entries and adjusted bank as the fuselage dot approached the horizon bar to establish a wings-level attitude. Each recovery was completed with heading inside 5 degrees and altitude inside 150 ft of the target values.
texts.4: SP interpreted the EADI presentation instantly on every entry, rolling the short way to the horizon indicated by the chevrons and blending the bank out exactly as the fuselage dot met the horizon bar. The aircraft arrived wings level with negligible heading and altitude deviation and no secondary roll input.

The deviations stayed close to the desired values. SP is expected to start reducing bank as the dot approaches the horizon bar so the aircraft arrives wings level without a correction.

error_modes.label: Termination of the recovery at normal instrument flight attitude

texts.0: SP, due to continuing the recovery input past the attitude required for normal instrument flight, pulled the nose well above the pitch band used in instrument flight and produced a second unusual attitude out of the first. The aircraft climbed more than 300 ft above the entry altitude with the airspeed more than 20 kt below the target. The IP took the controls to stop the over-recovery.
texts.1: SP, due to not identifying the point at which the recovery was complete, held the pull past level and left the aircraft with a pitch and bank outside the values used for normal instrument flight. SP stopped the input only after the IP called level. The altitude overshoot reached about 300 ft and the airspeed about 20 kt from the target, at the tolerance limits, without control intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to relaxing the recovery input slightly late, passed the desired attitude for normal instrument flight and had to make a small opposite correction to settle the aircraft. SP recognized the overshoot immediately and corrected it without prompting. The altitude overshoot was about 200 ft with the airspeed about 15 kt from the target.
texts.3: SP ended each recovery at the attitude required for normal instrument flight, with bank inside the normal instrument flight limit and pitch inside the normal band, and then held it. The altitude settled within 150 ft and the airspeed within 10 kt of the target values.
texts.4: SP stopped every recovery precisely at the normal instrument flight attitude with no overshoot in pitch or bank and no opposite correction afterwards. The aircraft was stabilized immediately with negligible altitude and airspeed deviation and the transition back to normal instrument flight was seamless.
texts.marginal: SP terminated each recovery inside the standards, but consistently passed slightly beyond the normal instrument flight attitude before settling, so every recovery contained a small opposite correction.
